title: Why Runaway Trucks Steer Into Gravel | How It Works #5

hook_candidates.text: This truck's brakes overheated. So why steer into gravel?
No brakes, a hundred kilometers an hour, and a pile of stones ahead.
Gravel stops a truck better than its brakes. Here's how.
Watch this speedometer. Loose stones have to bring it to zero.
Why are there gravel ramps on mountain highways?

hook_note: Tie between candidates 1 and 4; 1 chosen because its answer (the gravel swallows the wheels) comes latest and it states the problem the viewer has seen on mountain roads.

parts.text: This gravel must stop it in a hundred and fifty meters.
But these stones are round and loose.
Now every turn shoves gravel aside,
and that work eats the speed.
The deeper it sinks, the harder it plows,

sources: Brakes on long downgrades overheat and fade; a truck can accelerate until it runs off the road: Caltrans Traffic Bulletin No. 24, Design Guide for Truck Escape Ramps (1986), p. 1, https://dot.ca.gov/-/media/dot-media/programs/safety-programs/documents/safety-devices/19861001-tsb-24-design-guide-for-truck-escape-ramps-a11y-v3.pdf

Arrester-bed performance depends on the vehicle sinking into the gravel; washed, uncrushed, well-rounded gravel of uniform size; crushed, interlocking material lets the truck sink less and slow less; bed about 36 in deep; trucks sink at least 12 in: Caltrans TSB 24, pp. 7-9.

Stopping length L (ft) = V^2 / (30 (R + G)), V in mph; rolling resistance R: portland cement concrete 0.010, loose gravel 0.100, pea gravel 0.250 (AASHTO 1984 via Caltrans TSB 24, pp. 9-10). The bed resists about 25 times more than concrete (shown as bars, not spoken).

100 km/h = 62.1 mph on a level pea-gravel bed (G = 0): L = 62.1^2 / (30 x 0.25) = 515 ft = 157 m ('a hundred and fifty meters'). Labelled simplified model: level bed, no air drag, no engine braking. Arithmetic.
Bed uses rolling resistance to stop the vehicle: Wikipedia 'Runaway truck ramp', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runaway_truck_ramp
